meta.title: The Word at the Well-House
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses sensory words to bring a moment back.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 108w at FK 6.1, part_2 111w at FK 5.5. The load is sensory words, a long sentence with a dash, and the shift from action to realization.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Helen Keller, "The Story of My Life" (1903), Chapter IV, under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Keller, Helen. The Story of My Life. 1903. Project Gutenberg eBook #2397, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2397, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: Split the episode into two parts, changed 'Some one' to 'Someone', used an em dash, and simplified a few rare words; kept the author's sensory words; no facts added.
source.survey: A blind and deaf girl learns the word 'water' at a well-house.
source.avoided: No invented details about the teacher or the place.

session.difficulty_basis: sensory words, a long sentence with a dash, and the shift from action to realization

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: I felt my teacher sweep the pieces of the broken doll to one side of the hearth. I was glad the cause of my discomfort was gone. She brought me my hat, and I knew I was going out into the warm sunshine. We walked down the path to the well-house, drawn by the fragrance of the honeysuckle that covered it. Someone was drawing water, and my teacher placed my hand under the spout. As the cool stream gushed over one hand, she spelled into the other the word water, first slowly, then rapidly. I stood still, my whole attention fixed on the motions of her fingers.
passage.part_2: Suddenly I felt a strange feeling, as of something forgotten—a thrill of returning thought. Somehow the mystery of language opened to me. I knew then that "w-a-t-e-r" meant the wonderful cool something flowing over my hand. That living word awakened my soul; it gave me light, hope, and joy, and set me free. There were still barriers, but they could be swept away in time. I left the well-house eager to learn. Everything had a name, and each name gave birth to a new thought. As we walked back to the house, everything I touched seemed alive. I saw everything with a strange, new sight.

items.prompt: What did the teacher do with Helen's hand at the well-house?

tutor_only.confirm: She placed one hand under the spout and spelled 'water' into the other.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the teacher placed Helen's hand under the spout and spelled into the other hand as the water gushed.
tutor_only.tell: The teacher put one hand under the water and spelled the word into Helen's other hand.
help: Find the sentence that begins 'Someone was drawing water.'
Notice what the teacher did with each of Helen's hands.
tutor_only.core_idea: The teacher held Helen's hand under the water and spelled 'water' into her other hand.
accept_ideas: She placed one hand under the spout and spelled into the other.
The teacher spelled 'water' into Helen's hand while the water ran.
Helen's hand was under the water and the teacher spelled into her other hand.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the teacher was only drawing water.
if_they_say.ask: Who was drawing the water? What did the teacher do with Helen's hand?

items.prompt: What two things happened at the same time at the well-house?

tutor_only.confirm: Cool water gushed over one hand while the teacher spelled 'water' into the other.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence says the cool stream gushed over one hand as the teacher spelled into the other.
tutor_only.tell: The water ran over one hand while the teacher spelled the word into the other.
help: Look at the sentence about the cool stream.
Notice the two things happening at once.
tutor_only.core_idea: Water ran over one hand while the teacher spelled into the other.
accept_ideas: Water gushed over one hand while the teacher spelled into the other.
The teacher spelled the word as the water ran over Helen's hand.
Helen felt the water and the spelling at the same time.
not_required: Explaining why the water was cool
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They name only the water or only the spelling.
if_they_say.ask: What was happening to Helen's other hand at the same time?

tutor_only.confirm: She was fixing all her attention on the teacher's fingers.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says she stood still with her whole attention fixed on the motions of the teacher's fingers.
tutor_only.tell: Helen stood still because she was watching the teacher's fingers with all her attention.
help: Find the sentence that begins 'I stood still.'
Notice what her attention was fixed on.
tutor_only.core_idea: Helen stood still to give all her attention to the teacher's fingers.
accept_ideas: She was watching the teacher's fingers.
She fixed her attention on the motions of the fingers.
She was trying to understand what the fingers were doing.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say she was afraid or waiting for the water.
if_they_say.ask: What was Helen's attention fixed on?

items.prompt: 'Warm,' 'fragrance,' 'cool,' 'gushed' — what do those words do that a list of objects would not?

tutor_only.confirm: They name what the body meets there: heat, smell, cold water.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The words 'warm,' 'fragrance,' 'cool,' and 'gushed' appeal to touch and smell, so the moment feels vivid.
tutor_only.tell: The words name heat, a smell, and cold water, so the place reaches you through the body.
help: Notice which senses they speak to.
tutor_only.core_idea: The words name what the body meets — heat, a smell, cold water — so the place comes through the senses rather than as a list of objects.
accept_ideas: they name what the body meets, like heat and cold water
they use the senses rather than naming objects
the place comes through warmth and smell
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They define 'fragrance' or 'cool' without saying what the words do.
if_they_say.ask: What do those words help you feel or smell in this moment?

partial.when: the student says the words describe the garden or the place, without naming the senses
partial.ask: What do those four words name that a plain description of a garden would not?

items.prompt: The writer calls 'water' a 'living word.' What does that phrase make the word seem to do?

tutor_only.confirm: The phrase makes the word seem alive, able to wake her and set her free.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage calls 'water' a 'living word' that awakened her soul and set her free, so the phrase gives the word life and power, not only a name.
tutor_only.tell: She calls the word alive and says it awakened her soul. That makes water seem like a living thing.
help: Find the sentence that calls 'water' a living word.
Notice what the writer says that word did to her.
tutor_only.core_idea: The phrase makes the word seem alive, something that could wake her and set her free.
accept_ideas: It makes the word seem alive, like something that could wake her.
The word seems to act on her, not only name the water.
It makes water sound like a living thing that set her free.
not_required: Naming every word she learned that day
Explaining how she learned to read
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the word water is just a label for water.
if_they_say.ask: What does the writer say the living word did to her soul?
